item.title: Quantum RF Sensing
item.description: Quantum RF Sensing: A Reality Check Against a Real Link Budget In this post I work through the question: can a quantum RF receiver replace my traditional receiver? I had a perfect excuse to answer it. I was building a downlink for the GOES-R geosynchronous weather satellite, and the link budget was tight enough to make any noise-floor improvement worth chasing. So I looked hard at Rydberg-atom receivers, did the math, and came away with a nuanced answer. This post walks you through what I found, with equations, scaling laws, and a couple of scripts you can run yourself.

item.title: Collecting L-band Satellite Signals
item.description: In the past, I have captured signals at 137.1 MHz from the NOAA 19 weather satellite using a discone antenna without any pointing. It was exciting to see weather images apear on the computer monitor after processing the signals. At the time, I planned to find a way to setup a tracking capability so I could track the satellites while pointing a higher gain antenna at them to get better signal-to-noise-ratios (SNR) and longer collection time. Well, I have finally put together a system that can do this for L-band and UHF frequenies. A system adequate for x-band is in the works.

item.title: From Vision to Prototype
item.description:
This post describes my teaching and mentoring approach that has evolved over the past decade through mentoring new engineering hires and summer interns. The approach emphasizes system-level thinking, project-driven learning, and just-in-time introduction of theoretical principles, with the aim of bridging the gap between classroom instruction and the realities of engineering practice.

The method unfolds in four stages: establishing a vision, decomposing into subsystems, cycling between systems and principles, and validating through demonstration.

item.title: Observing Satellites
item.description:
Observing satellites in the night sky can be a fun way to learn about orbital dynamics and learn your way around the earth and sky. This discussion is specific to observers in the northern hemisphere since I am currently living in the Rocky Mountain West area.

First, let’s review some important terminology:

Azimuth is the horizontal angle, measured in degrees, from true north in a clockwise direction. The star Polaris lies within one degree of true north and is therefore a useful reference point for determining azimuth in the night sky. To locate Polaris, first find the Big Dipper (Ursa Major) and identify the two stars that form the far edge of the dipper’s cup. Extending an imaginary line through these stars about five times their spacing will point to Polaris, a magnitude~+2 star. Because of the geometry of Earth’s rotation, Polaris appears at an altitude approximately equal to the observer’s latitude.

item.title: Intuitive Derivations in DSP
item.description:
One of the most important concepts in digital signal processing is that a Linear-Time-Invariant (LTI) system is completely characterized in the time-domain by the output response to a unit impulse input. This can be imagined as probing the input of an LTI system with a Kronecker delta function and then determining the resulting output. $$ \delta[n] \rightarrow \boxed{LTI} \rightarrow h[n] $$

In this simple diagram, the output function $h[n]$ is called the “impulse response” of the system.

item.title: Time-Frequency Analysis of Non-Stationary Signals
item.description:
Check out the Matlab demo code to explore time-frequency analysis using a Bat signal…not the super-hero one.

Often, the examples provided in our signal processing textbooks assume that the signal we are working with is wide-sense-stationary. This means that the first and second order statistics (mean and correlation) do not change with shifts in time. Although, all of our statistical signal processing techniques depend upon this statistical behavior in order to produce meaningful characterizations when analyzing a random signal, many real-world signals don’t have nonstationary characteristics. A bat echo-location signal is just one example.

item.title: Machine Learning 101
item.description:
In real-world signal processing and machine learning, we often deal with uncertain or even stochastic (i.e. non-deterministic) quantities. There are three main sources of uncertainty worth mentioning:

  1. Inherent stochastic systems — e.g. the dynamics of sub-atomic particles.
  2. Incomplete observations — Even deterministic systems appear stochastic when we cannot observe all the variables that drive the system’s behavior.
  3. Incomplete modeling — When we model a system but discard information we have observed (e.g. discrete sampling of position).

item.title: Fast Correlation
item.description:
There are two methods for computing the correlation of complex-valued signals. The first one is a time-domain method, and for a stationary process can be computed using the following formula

$$ r(k) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{N} \sum^{N-k-1}_{n=0} x(n+k)h^{\ast}(n) & \text{if } 0 \leq k \leq N-1 \\ r^{\ast}(-k) & \text{if } -(N-1) \leq k \lt 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } elsewhere \end{cases} $$

where N is the input data record length, x(n) is the input data and h(n) is the kernel, or reference data. The computational time to compute a correlation using this method is directly proportional to the number of samples in the kernel. Therefore, the longer the kernel data record the more time it takes to compute a correlation.

item.title: Deep Learning with Radio Frequency Signals
item.description: Signal Classification Using Spectrograms and Deep Learning In this post, I will introduce some basic methods for utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to process spectrograms created from Radio Frequency (RF) data. The information in the post was taken from a tutorial my colleagues and I provided to NVidia Corporation in early 2015 that has been used in their enterprise training series for several years. This post links you to a git project that removes the dependency on Nvidia’s DIGITS platform and uses only Keras and Tensorflow. Project Code & Data
